prompt: In this course, when does an item's cycle time start and stop?

choices.text: From the day the request is written down until it reaches production
choices.why: That is lead time, the requester's clock.

choices.text: From the day somebody starts it until its change merges
choices.why: Right. Cycle time is the team's clock, from start to merge.

choices.text: From the first commit until that commit runs in production
choices.why: That is DORA's lead time for changes, which lesson 5 measures.

choices.text: From review until merge
choices.why: That is only the review column, one part of cycle time.

prompt: Match each clock to the moment it starts.
A team measures lead time from the day each idea was written into a backlog full of ideas that are never built. What is wrong with that?

choices.text: Lead time should be measured in working days
choices.why: Calendar or working days is a separate choice; it does not fix where the clock starts.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as the board records the dates
choices.why: Recorded dates do not help when the clock starts on things nobody agreed to do.

choices.text: It makes the number too small to be useful
choices.why: It makes it large and flattering at once, not small.

choices.text: The clock runs on unagreed work, and only finished items report
choices.why: Right. Start at the commitment point instead, where the team agrees the item will be done.

prompt: The moment a team agrees an item will be done, often a column called Ready, is the ___ point.
An item started on 1 September and merged on 3 September. What is its cycle time in days, counted the way this course counts?
Why does an average cycle time describe the typical item badly?

choices.text: A few very slow items pull it up
choices.why: Right. The distribution leans right with a long tail, and the mean follows the tail.

choices.text: It is computed only from items that were blocked
choices.why: It uses every finished item in the period.

choices.text: It counts weekends, which most teams do not work
choices.why: Weekends affect every summary equally; the problem is the shape of the distribution.

choices.text: Averages can only be taken over equal-sized items
choices.why: Any numbers can be averaged; skewed ones are just poorly described by it.

prompt: Twenty items have these cycle times in days, sorted: 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 15, 21, 30. What is the 85th percentile by nearest rank?
In September the Billing team's cycle times had a mean of 5.0 days and an 85th percentile of 8. Which sentence can it honestly say to a stakeholder?

choices.text: Every item will be finished within five days
choices.why: Eight of thirty items took longer than five days in September.

choices.text: No item will take more than eight days
choices.why: The 85th percentile leaves 15% above it; one item took 17 days.

choices.text: 85% of our items finish within eight days
choices.why: Right. A percentile turned into a sentence about the team's own history: a service level expectation.

choices.text: Our items take five days, give or take a day or two
choices.why: The spread runs from one day to seventeen; give or take two hides most of it.

prompt: A team with 25 finished items in a month quotes its 95th-percentile cycle time in a planning meeting. Why is that number weak?

choices.text: The 95th percentile is always lower than the mean
choices.why: In a right-leaning distribution it is far above the mean.

choices.text: It rests on one or two items, so one straggler moves it
choices.why: Right. With 25 items the 95th is the second-longest; quote it after fifty or so.

choices.text: Percentiles can only be computed for a whole quarter
choices.why: Any period works; the problem is how few items sit above the 95th.

choices.text: Stakeholders only understand averages
choices.why: A sentence like 85% within eight days is easy to understand; the issue is sample size.

prompt: What is a service level expectation in the Kanban Guide's sense?

choices.text: A deadline the team must meet for every item it starts
choices.why: It is not a deadline for any one item.

choices.text: A contract with customers that carries penalties
choices.why: That is closer to an SLA; an SLE is the team's own forecast.

choices.text: The average cycle time over the last quarter
choices.why: An SLE pairs a cycle time with a probability, which an average does not have.

choices.text: A cycle time and the chance of meeting it
choices.why: Right. Such as: 85% of items finish within eight days.

prompt: On the Billing team's scatterplot, August shows tall dots next to short ones. What are the tall ones?

choices.text: Items started under the old rules, still finishing
choices.why: Right. Their start dates are before 3 August; they are the old system draining out.

choices.text: Evidence that the new rules made every item slower
choices.why: Items started after the change all finished within eight days.

choices.text: Items that were blocked and are still open
choices.why: An open item has no dot: a dot appears only when an item finishes.

choices.text: Bugs, which always take longer than features
choices.why: The chart does not split by type, and nothing says bugs take longer.

prompt: Why does BIL-189, open and blocked since 21 August, not appear on the cycle-time scatterplot?

choices.text: Blocked items are removed from the data before plotting
choices.why: Nothing is removed; the chart has no place for it yet.

choices.text: It is a bug, and the chart shows only features
choices.why: Every type is plotted.

choices.text: A dot appears only when an item finishes
choices.why: Right. The scatterplot's blind spot is exactly the item that is not finishing; lesson 3 draws it.

choices.text: Its cycle time is too long to fit on the axis
choices.why: It has no cycle time at all, because it has not merged.

prompt: Which questions does a cycle-time scatterplot answer quickly? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: Has something changed in how long items take?
choices.why: Right. A shift in where the dots sit shows before a percentile moves.

choices.text: Which finished items deserve a conversation?
choices.why: Right. The dots above the 85th-percentile line.

choices.text: Which developer is the slowest?
choices.why: The dots are items, and the question about an item is what happened, not who.

choices.text: How old are the items still open?
choices.why: Open items have no dot; that is the ageing chart in lesson 3.

prompt: In June and July, an item spent 7.1 days in the review column on average. What was most of that time?

choices.text: Careful reviewing of large changes
choices.why: A review takes hours; the days were spent before anybody picked it up.

choices.text: Waiting in a queue for the one reviewer
choices.why: Right. Bia reviewed everything between her other duties, and the queue in front of her grew.

choices.text: Rework after reviews that found problems
choices.why: billing.py models no rework; the time is queueing.

choices.text: Waiting for Thursday's deployment
choices.why: That wait is its own column, after the merge: 2.7 days.

prompt: In September an item deployed by the Billing team spent 27.3 of its 32.5 days of lead time in the backlog. What percentage is that, to the nearest whole number?
The Billing team's cycle time fell from 19 days to 5, yet the requester's lead time fell only from 42.5 to 32.5. Why?

choices.text: The September deployments were slower than the Thursday ones
choices.why: The wait to deploy fell from 2.7 days to a few hours.

choices.text: The new rules made development take longer
choices.why: Development fell from 11.9 days to 3.6.

choices.text: Lead time is measured in working days and cycle time in calendar days
choices.why: Both are calendar days in this course.

choices.text: A queue built up in July still sat in the backlog
choices.why: Right. About twenty requests waited in front of a team finishing one a day: some twenty days of wait.

prompt: Once the work inside a team moves quickly, which move shortens a requester's wait the most?

choices.text: Keep the backlog short, and decline what will not be done soon
choices.why: Right. The backlog has become the biggest queue; shortening it shortens lead time.

choices.text: Ask developers to work faster on each item
choices.why: Development is already a small share; speed there buys little.

choices.text: Deploy twice a day instead of once
choices.why: Waiting to deploy is already hours out of a month.

choices.text: Add a second review per item
choices.why: That lengthens the review column and does nothing to the backlog.

prompt: Put the four stretches of an item's lead time in the order the item passes through them.
An item was actively worked on for 2 days out of a cycle time of 8 days. What is its flow efficiency, in percent?
Why can't the Billing team's files compute its flow efficiency?

choices.text: The files do not record when items were started
choices.why: They record started, review and merged for every item.

choices.text: Flow efficiency needs at least a year of data
choices.why: It needs a different kind of data, not more of it.

choices.text: A board records column changes, not when work happened
choices.why: Right. Nobody moves a card each time they stop working on it, so active time is not in the data.

choices.text: The simulation has no waiting in it
choices.why: It is mostly waiting; the board just does not say which days were work.

prompt: A team splits Development into doing and done. What does the done half let the board measure?

choices.text: How many hours each developer works
choices.why: Columns measure items, not people's hours.

choices.text: Time spent finished and waiting for review
choices.why: Right. Time in a done column is waiting by definition, and now the board counts it.

choices.text: Which items were estimated wrongly
choices.why: Estimates are lesson 9's subject; the split measures waiting.

choices.text: The flow efficiency of the whole team exactly
choices.why: It measures one queue; waiting inside the doing half is still invisible.

prompt: A manager sees a flow efficiency of 15% and proposes that developers track their hours more strictly to be busier. What does the lesson say about that?

choices.text: It is right: low flow efficiency means people are idle
choices.why: Low flow efficiency means items wait, usually while people are busy with other items.

choices.text: It works as long as the hours are tracked per item
choices.why: Per-item hours measure the 15%; the gain is in the other 85%.

choices.text: It is needed before anything else can be measured
choices.why: The lesson measured waiting from the board alone, with no hours at all.

choices.text: It is aimed at people, and the waiting belongs to the system
choices.why: Right. The fix is fewer items open and faster hand-offs, not busier people.

prompt: A report says "lead time went down by half this quarter". What should you ask first?

choices.text: Which clock, and where does it start?
choices.why: Right. Cycle time, lead time and lead time for changes are different clocks, and a moved start looks like an improvement.

choices.text: Who on the team worked hardest?
choices.why: A lead time is a property of the system, not of a person.

choices.text: Whether the number was rounded correctly
choices.why: Rounding cannot halve a number; a different definition can.

choices.text: How many items were estimated in points
choices.why: Estimates do not enter any of the three clocks.

prompt: A percentile computed by nearest ___ is always a value that really happened.
